title: Why Money Exists
content:
Money 101: What even IS money?
Lesson: Why Money Exists
Concept Card 1: Trading goods directly without money. E.g., 5 apples for 2 eggs. Problem: You need someone who wants exactly what you have!
Concept Card 2: A medium of exchange — something everyone agrees has value. It solves the barter problem by being accepted by everyone.
Concept Card 3: 1. Medium of Exchange (buy/sell things)
2. Unit of Account (measure value)
3. Store of Value (save for later)
Concept Card 4: There isn't enough of everything for everyone. Scarcity is the fundamental reason economics exists.
Quick Recap: What is Barter? | What is Money? | 3 Functions of Money

options: Solves the double coincidence of wants in barter

title: Nepali Currency: The Rupee
content:
Money 101: What even IS money?
Lesson: Nepali Currency: The Rupee
Concept Card 1: Nepali Rupee — Nepal's official currency. Symbol: रू or Rs. Issued by Nepal Rastra Bank (NRB).
Concept Card 2: Nepal's central bank, established 1956. Controls money supply, sets interest rates, and maintains currency stability.
Concept Card 3: How much of one currency you get for another. E.g., 1 USD ≈ 133 NPR. Rates change daily based on trade and market forces.
Concept Card 4: Because Nepal imports more than it exports, trade imbalance weakens NPR. Also tied closely to Indian Rupee (INR).

title: Inflation: Why Things Get Expensive
content:
Money 101: What even IS money?
Lesson: Inflation: Why Things Get Expensive
Concept Card 1: The general rise in prices over time. If momo cost Rs.50 last year and Rs.60 now — that's 20% inflation on momos!
Concept Card 2: 1. Too much money chasing too few goods
2. Supply disruptions (less goods)
3. Demand surge (more buyers)
4. Import costs rising
Concept Card 3: Consumer Price Index — measures inflation by tracking prices of a 'basket' of everyday goods like rice, oil, vegetables, transport.
Concept Card 4: Your Rs.1,000 buys less every year. Savings lose purchasing power. Fixed-income earners suffer most.
Concept Card 5: Mild inflation (2-4%) = healthy economy. High inflation (10%+) = economic stress. Deflation (negative) = also bad — people stop spending.
Quick Recap: What is Inflation? | What causes Inflation? | What is CPI?

quiz.prompt: If your salary stays at Rs.50,000 but inflation is 10%, what happens?

title: How Banks Work
content:
Banking Basics: Where does your money go?
Lesson: How Banks Work
Concept Card 1: Banks take deposits from savers and lend that money to borrowers. They charge borrowers more interest than they pay savers — that's their profit.
Concept Card 2: Banks only keep a fraction of deposits in cash. The rest is loaned out. If you deposit Rs.100, the bank might lend Rs.90 and keep Rs.10.
Concept Card 3: When everyone tries to withdraw their money at once. Banks can't fulfill this because money is lent out. This caused collapses in the Great Depression.
Concept Card 4: 1. Commercial Banks (e.g., NIC Asia, Nabil)
2. Development Banks
3. Finance Companies
4. Microfinance Institutions
5. Nepal Rastra Bank (central bank)
Quick Recap: What do banks actually do? | What is Fractional Reserve Banking? | What is a Bank Run?

options: Charging higher interest to borrowers than they pay savers
Banks lend out most deposits, keeping only a fraction

title: Savings vs Fixed Deposits
content:
Banking Basics: Where does your money go?
Lesson: Savings vs Fixed Deposits
Concept Card 1: Flexible account. Withdraw anytime. Low interest (2-4% in Nepal). Good for emergency funds and daily expenses.
Concept Card 2: Lock money for fixed period (3 months to 5 years). Higher interest (7-11% in Nepal). Penalty if withdrawn early.
Concept Card 3: Depends on goal:
• Need money soon → Savings Account
• Won't need money for 1+ year → Fixed Deposit
• Best strategy: Keep 3 months expenses in savings, rest in FD
Concept Card 4: Real Return = Interest Rate - Inflation Rate
If FD gives 8% but inflation is 7%, your real return is just 1%. You barely grew your money!
Quick Recap: Savings Account | Fixed Deposit (FD) | Which is better?

title: Loans, EMI & Interest
content:
Banking Basics: Where does your money go?
Lesson: Loans, EMI & Interest
Concept Card 1: Equated Monthly Installment. Fixed amount paid every month to repay a loan. Includes both principal and interest.
Concept Card 2: Simple: Interest only on principal
Compound: Interest on principal + previous interest
Compound grows MUCH faster. Good for investing, bad for loans.
Concept Card 3: Good Debt: Builds wealth (education loan, home loan)
Bad Debt: Loses value (loan for gadgets, luxury)
Worst Debt: High-interest consumer loans (30%+ APR)
Concept Card 4: Credit Information Bureau (CIB) tracks your loan repayment history. Good score = lower interest rates on future loans. Bad score = harder to borrow.
Quick Recap: What is EMI? | Simple vs Compound Interest | Good Debt vs Bad Debt

title: Income, Expenses & Budget
content:
Personal Finance: Master your own money first
Lesson: Income, Expenses & Budget
Concept Card 1: Your take-home pay AFTER taxes. If salary is Rs.60,000 and tax is Rs.5,000, net income = Rs.55,000.
Concept Card 2: 50% → Needs (rent, food, transport)
30% → Wants (eating out, Netflix)
20% → Savings & debt repayment
A simple budget framework.
Concept Card 3: Fixed: Same every month (rent, loan EMI)
Variable: Changes monthly (groceries, entertainment)
Control variable expenses to save more.
Concept Card 4: Assign every rupee a job. Income - All Expenses = 0. Not because you spend everything, but because every rupee is allocated to SOMETHING (including savings).
Quick Recap: What is Net Income? | 50/30/20 Rule | Fixed vs Variable Expenses

title: Emergency Fund: Your Safety Net
content:
Personal Finance: Master your own money first
Lesson: Emergency Fund: Your Safety Net
Concept Card 1: Money saved specifically for unexpected events: job loss, medical emergency, urgent repair. NOT for sales, trips, or impulse buys.
Concept Card 2: 3-6 months of your monthly expenses. If you spend Rs.30,000/month, target Rs.90,000-1,80,000 in emergency fund.
Concept Card 3: High-interest savings account or liquid mutual fund. NOT in stocks (can crash when you need it most). Must be accessible within 1-2 days.
Concept Card 4: According to studies, most Nepalis can't cover a Rs.10,000 emergency without borrowing. Remittance-dependent families are especially vulnerable if the main earner falls ill.
Quick Recap: What is an Emergency Fund? | How much should you save? | Where to keep emergency fund?

title: FOMO, Lifestyle Inflation & Traps
content:
Personal Finance: Master your own money first
Lesson: FOMO, Lifestyle Inflation & Traps
Concept Card 1: Fear of Missing Out. Seeing friends buy iPhones, go to Maldives, drive new cars — and feeling pressure to match them. Leads to overspending and debt.
Concept Card 2: When income rises, expenses rise to match it. Earned Rs.10,000 more? Suddenly 'need' a better phone, fancier food, pricier rent. Net savings = same as before.
Concept Card 3: Social media shows you the highlight reel. That friend in Maldives might have credit card debt. That new car might be on a 7-year loan. Compare outcomes, not appearances.
Concept Card 4: Continuing something bad because you already invested in it. 'I paid Rs.5,000 for this course so I must finish it.' The Rs.5,000 is gone either way — make the best decision NOW.
Quick Recap: What is FOMO? | Lifestyle Inflation | The Comparison Trap

options: Expenses growing as fast as income, with no net savings gain
Continuing a bad decision because of past investment
Compare your financial progress to your own past self

title: What is the Share Market?
content:
Nepal Share Market: NEPSE — Nepal's stock exchange
Lesson: What is the Share Market?
Concept Card 1: A small ownership piece of a company. If Nabil Bank has 1 crore shares and you own 100, you own 0.0001% of Nabil Bank and share in its profits.
Concept Card 2: Nepal Stock Exchange. Nepal's only stock exchange where shares are bought and sold. Located in Kathmandu, established in 1993.
Concept Card 3: To raise capital (money) from the public without taking loans. You give them money; they give you ownership shares. Win-win if the company grows.
Concept Card 4: Bull Market: Prices rising, optimism, everyone buying
Bear Market: Prices falling, fear, everyone selling
NEPSE has experienced both dramatically — 2020-21 was a major bull run.
Quick Recap: What is a Share? | What is NEPSE? | Why do companies list on NEPSE?

title: IPO: Getting In Early
content:
Nepal Share Market: NEPSE — Nepal's stock exchange
Lesson: IPO: Getting In Early
Concept Card 1: Initial Public Offering. The FIRST time a company sells shares to the public. Nepal's IPO culture is massive — people apply hoping for allotment and quick profit.
Concept Card 2: 1. Open DEMAT account (Mero Share)
2. Link bank account
3. Apply via Mero Share app during open window
4. Pay application amount
5. Wait for allotment lottery
Concept Card 3: Dematerialized account — stores your shares electronically. Like a bank account but for stocks. Required to trade on NEPSE. Opened through brokers or banks.
Concept Card 4: In Nepal, IPOs are massively oversubscribed (10x-100x demand). So it's a lottery. Applying for more units doesn't help — it's 1 unit per application.
Concept Card 5: Shares start trading on NEPSE secondary market. Price can go up (profit) or down (loss) from issue price. Many Nepali IPOs list above issue price — but not always.
Quick Recap: What is IPO? | How to Apply for IPO in Nepal? | What is DEMAT Account?

title: Reading Share Prices & Indicators
content:
Nepal Share Market: NEPSE — Nepal's stock exchange
Lesson: Reading Share Prices & Indicators
Concept Card 1: A number representing the overall value of all NEPSE-listed shares. If NEPSE index rises from 2000 to 2200, the market overall gained 10%.
Concept Card 2: Total value of a company = Share Price × Total Shares. E.g., if Nabil Bank has 10 crore shares at Rs.1000 each, market cap = Rs.10 arba.
Concept Card 3: Price-to-Earnings Ratio. How much you pay per rupee of profit.
P/E = Share Price ÷ Earnings Per Share
Lower P/E = potentially cheaper. High P/E = market expects high growth.
Concept Card 4: Earnings Per Share. Company's annual profit ÷ number of shares. EPS of Rs.50 means the company earned Rs.50 per share this year.
Concept Card 5: A portion of company profit given to shareholders. Nepal banks often give 10-25% dividends. Types: Cash dividend (actual money) or Stock dividend (extra shares).
Quick Recap: What is NEPSE Index? | What is Market Capitalization? | What is P/E Ratio?

title: Types of Companies on NEPSE
content:
Nepal Share Market: NEPSE — Nepal's stock exchange
Lesson: Types of Companies on NEPSE
Concept Card 1: Largest sector on NEPSE. Commercial banks like Nabil, NIC Asia, Standard Chartered. Generally stable with regular dividends. Regulated by NRB.
Concept Card 2: Nepal's growing sector. Companies like Upper Tamakoshi, NHPC. Long construction phase, then stable revenue. Connected to Nepal's energy future.
Concept Card 3: Life and non-life insurance companies. Life insurance: Nepal Life, NLGI. Regulated by Insurance Board (Beema Samiti).
Concept Card 4: Development banks and finance companies. Higher risk, potentially higher return. Microfinance serves rural Nepal — some listed on NEPSE.
Concept Card 5: Companies like Bottlers Nepal (Coca-Cola), Unilever Nepal. Smaller sector on NEPSE but growing.

title: Risk & Return
content:
Investing Principles: Think like an investor
Lesson: Risk & Return
Concept Card 1: Higher potential return = higher risk. FD: Low risk, low return. Stocks: High risk, high potential return. No free lunch in investing.
Concept Card 2: Market risk: Overall market falls
Company risk: Specific company fails
Liquidity risk: Can't sell when you want
Inflation risk: Returns don't beat inflation
Concept Card 3: Don't put all eggs in one basket. Spread across sectors (banking + hydro + insurance) and asset types (stocks + FD + gold). If one falls, others cushion the blow.
Concept Card 4: How long you can leave money invested. Short term (under 3 years): Low risk instruments. Long term (10+ years): Can afford more volatility for higher returns.
Quick Recap: Risk-Return Relationship | Types of Investment Risk | Diversification

title: Mutual Funds in Nepal
content:
Investing Principles: Think like an investor
Lesson: Mutual Funds in Nepal
Concept Card 1: Pool of money from many investors, managed by a professional fund manager. They invest in stocks, bonds, etc. You get units representing your share.
Concept Card 2: NEPSE has listed mutual funds. Examples: Nabil Equity Fund, Laxmi Value Fund, NMB Saral Bachat. Minimum investment often as low as Rs.1,000.
Concept Card 3: Price per unit of a mutual fund. If NAV is Rs.12 and you invest Rs.12,000, you get 1,000 units. NAV changes daily based on fund's portfolio.
Concept Card 4: Active: Manager picks stocks, trying to beat market. Higher fees.
Passive: Tracks an index (like NEPSE index). Lower fees. Research shows passive often outperforms active long-term.

title: Warren Buffett's Rules
content:
Investing Principles: Think like an investor
Lesson: Warren Buffett's Rules
Concept Card 1: Rule #2: Never forget Rule #1. Protecting capital matters more than chasing gains. Losing 50% requires 100% gain just to recover.
Concept Card 2: Only invest in businesses you understand. Buffett avoided tech stocks for decades because he didn't understand their moat. He understood Coca-Cola — simple, consistent, global.
Concept Card 3: 'Our favorite holding period is forever.' Great companies compound over decades. Short-term trading is expensive (taxes, fees) and emotionally exhausting.
Concept Card 4: Benjamin Graham's idea: Imagine Mr. Market comes daily offering to buy or sell. He's sometimes euphoric (overpriced) and sometimes depressed (underpriced). Your job: Don't follow his mood. Buy when he's scared.
Concept Card 5: Know what you know. Know what you don't know. Only invest in areas within your competence. Expand the circle slowly but never pretend it's bigger than it is.
Quick Recap: Rule #1: Never Lose Money | Buy What You Understand | Long-Term Thinking

title: Technical Analysis Basics
content:
Advanced NEPSE: Trade smart, not hard
Lesson: Technical Analysis Basics
Concept Card 1: Studying past price charts and patterns to predict future price movements. Based on the idea that price patterns repeat. Used by traders (not long-term investors).
Concept Card 2: Support: Price level where stock tends to stop falling (buyers step in)
Resistance: Price level where stock tends to stop rising (sellers step in)
Breaking these levels is significant.
Concept Card 3: Average price over a period (50-day MA, 200-day MA). If short-term MA crosses above long-term MA = 'Golden Cross' (bullish). Opposite = 'Death Cross' (bearish).
Concept Card 4: Number of shares traded. High volume on price rise = strong move. High volume on price fall = panic selling. Low volume moves are less reliable.
Concept Card 5: Measures if stock is overbought or oversold. RSI above 70 = overbought (may fall). RSI below 30 = oversold (may rise). Range: 0-100.
Quick Recap: What is Technical Analysis? | Support & Resistance | Moving Averages

options: Short-term MA crosses above long-term MA

title: Fundamental Analysis for NEPSE
content:
Advanced NEPSE: Trade smart, not hard
Lesson: Fundamental Analysis for NEPSE
Concept Card 1: Evaluating a company's actual business health: revenues, profits, debt, management quality. Used to find undervalued stocks to buy and hold.
Concept Card 2: NPA (Non-Performing Assets %): Lower is better — shows loan quality
CDR (Credit to Deposit Ratio): NRB mandates under 90%
ROE (Return on Equity): How efficiently using shareholder money
Concept Card 3: Company's net assets ÷ shares. If BV = Rs.200 and share price = Rs.150, it's trading BELOW book value — potentially undervalued. Price-to-Book ratio < 1 often seen as cheap.
Concept Card 4: Key sections to check:
• Chairman's message (vision)
• Financial statements (profit/loss)
• Notes to accounts (hidden details)
• Auditor's report (red flags)
Available on NEPSE website for all listed companies.

title: Rights Shares & Bonus Shares
content:
Advanced NEPSE: Trade smart, not hard
Lesson: Rights Shares & Bonus Shares
Concept Card 1: Existing shareholders get the 'right' to buy new shares at a discounted price. E.g., 1:10 rights means for every 10 shares you own, you can buy 1 new share at Rs.100 (vs market price of Rs.500).
Concept Card 2: Free shares given from company's reserves. 20% bonus = for every 100 shares, you get 20 more free. Share price adjusts down proportionally — but you have more shares.
Concept Card 3: Not exactly. If 20% bonus, share price drops ~20% on ex-date. Your total value stays roughly same. But long-term, if company keeps earning well, more shares = more dividends later.
Concept Card 4: Date when company records who owns shares for dividends/bonuses. Own shares BEFORE this date to qualify. After this, price drops by roughly dividend amount (ex-dividend date).
Quick Recap: What are Rights Shares? | What are Bonus Shares? | Does Bonus = Free Money?
